newsitem.title: USA: Silver more volatile than gold in 1996--Gold Field.
newsitem.headline: Silver more volatile than gold in 1996--Gold Field.

text.p: Silver was again more volatile than gold in 1996, with silver trading a range of 21 percent of its average price of $5.20 an ounce against 12 percent for gold, said Gold Field Mineral Services Ltd in its 1997 "World Silver Survey" published Wednesday on behalf of Silver Institute.
"It is clear that the price of silver has been much more volatile than that of gold over the past five years," one of the report's authors, Philip Klapwijk, told analysts and journalists in New York.
Comparing the ratio of gold and silver's volatities for 1996, silver tended to show daily movement of almost three times as much as gold, Klapwijk said.

"There have been only three years since 1968 (1973, 1978 and 1990) when the volatility of silver was not significantly above that of gold (that is the ratio of the volatilities was greater than one)," he said.
However, there is a strong correlation in the price direction of the two metals, with silver moving the same direction as gold in 80 percent of the trading days in 1996.

But for most of 1996, the price of silver was cheap relative to gold, with the gold/silver ratio rising to around 80:1. That meant silver fell faster than gold, although the ratio remained below its record high of 100.8:1 set Feb 25, 1991.

But the strength of the dollar last year masked the improvement in silver's supply and demand fundamentals, and weak gold prices affected investment interest in silver too, according to the Gold Field report.
"In fact, the average price (of silver) in many countries and currencies actually improved year-on-year, in some cases quite significantly," Klapwijk said.
After setting a high at $5.8275 on Feb 2, 1996, spot silver declined to a year's low of $4.71 on Dec 3.
Since then, silver recovered to a high of $5.40 on March 3 before slipping to a two-year low of $4.60 in late April.
Above-ground stocks of silver again eroded in 1996 due to a continued deficit between mine production and scrap supply on the one hand, and fabrication demand on the other, the GFMS report stated.
"In 1996, the resulting gap widened substantially to 160 million ounces (or nearly 5,000 tonnes), but this was still below the record of 180 million ounces (5,600 tonnes) set in 1993," Klapwijk said.

"The increase in the gap last year was not due to any decline in supply from mine production or scrap recycling, both of which rose modestly, but was, instead, a result of the 4.5 percent increase in fabrication demand," he added.

The main components of above-ground stocks which bridged the gap were private disinvestment of 149 million ounces (4,600 tonnes) and official sector sales of 23 million ounces (715 tonnes), according to the report.

"The evidence...suggests the market is moving in the direction of a genuine tightening, with identifiable stocks now approximately equal to four years of the supply/demand gap recorded in 1996," Klapwijk said.
